say: You give it a function, $f(x)$, and a point on its graph. It gives back the **tangent** there: the straight line that just touches the curve.
The key idea: the **slope** of the tangent at $x = a$ is $f'(a)$. Once you have the slope and the point, it is just the equation of a line.

how.higher: Higher level asks it on Paper 1 as a 10-mark part (2016, 2018, 2021, 2023, 2024, 2025), usually with a trig or exponential function, and sometimes only to find an unknown such as $k$ from the tangent.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks it on Paper 1, mostly in Q4 (2016, 2020, 2022, 2023, 2025): the previous part finds $f'(x)$, then a 5-mark part finds the slope or the line.

example.question: The curve $y = x^3 - 3x + 1$ has a point where $x = 2$. Find the equation of the tangent to the curve at that point.

steps.title: Find the slope
steps.say: The slope of the tangent is the derivative at $x = 2$. Differentiate, then put in $x = 2$.

steps.title: Find the point
steps.say: The tangent touches the curve, so it passes through the point on the curve where $x = 2$. Put $x = 2$ into the original function, not the derivative.

steps.title: Write the equation
steps.say: Now use the slope $\hl{1}{9}$ and the point $(2, \hl{2}{3})$ in the formula for a line.

say: You give it a curve and a slope $m$, or a line the tangent must be parallel to. It finds the **points** on the curve where the tangent has that slope.
The key idea: set the derivative equal to $m$ and solve. Parallel lines have the same slope.

how.higher: Higher level has asked it once on Paper 1, in 2024 Q3(c): a 15-mark part where you draw tangents parallel to a given line and read off the $x$-values.

example.question: The tangent to the curve $y = x^3 - 6x^2 + 5$ is parallel to the line $y = -9x + 4$ at two points. Find the $x$-coordinates of these two points.

steps.title: Find the slope wanted
steps.say: Parallel lines have equal slopes. The line $y = -9x + 4$ has slope $\hl{1}{-9}$, so the tangent must too.

steps.title: Differentiate the curve
steps.say: The slope of the tangent at any point is $\frac{dy}{dx}$.

steps.title: Set the slope equal
steps.say: Set $\frac{dy}{dx}$ equal to $\hl{1}{-9}$ and solve the quadratic.

steps.title: Read off the x-values
steps.say: Each bracket gives one point where the tangent has slope $-9$.

lines.text: Putting these into the curve gives the points $(1, 0)$ and $(3, -22)$.

say: You give it a function and an $x$ value. It tells you whether the function is **increasing** or **decreasing** there.
The key idea: look at the sign of $f'(a)$. If it is positive the graph is rising. If it is negative the graph is falling.

how.higher: Higher level asks it on Paper 1 as a 5 to 10-mark part inside a longer question (2018, 2019, 2022, 2023), often about a real situation such as a rate, where you must use calculus and state the conclusion.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks it on Paper 1 Q4 (2022, 2025): you match points on a graph to $f'(x) < 0$, $= 0$ and $> 0$, and give a reason.

example.question: $f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5$. Use differentiation to decide whether $f$ is increasing or decreasing at $x = 1$.

steps.title: Differentiate
steps.say: The slope of the graph is given by the derivative, so find $f'(x)$ first.

steps.title: Find the slope at x = 1
steps.say: Put $x = 1$ into the derivative, not into $f(x)$.

steps.title: Say what the sign means
steps.say: The slope $\hl{1}{-4}$ is negative, so the graph is falling at $x = 1$. Write the conclusion in words.

lines.text: Slope is negative, so $f$ is **decreasing** at $x = 1$.

say: You give it a function. It finds the values of $x$ where the function is **increasing** ($f'(x) > 0$) or **decreasing** ($f'(x) < 0$).
The key idea: turn the question into an inequality in $f'(x)$. If $f'(x)$ is always positive, the function is increasing for every $x$.

how.higher: Higher level has asked it on Paper 1 as a 10-mark part (2022 Q5(b)(ii)): differentiate the cubic, solve the quadratic inequality $f'(x) < 0$ with the formula and give the range.

example.question: Show that $f(x) = x^3 + 3x^2 + 5x - 4$ is increasing for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

steps.title: Differentiate
steps.say: A function is increasing where $f'(x) > 0$. Start by finding $f'(x)$.

steps.title: Complete the square
steps.say: A quadratic with no real roots does not cross the axis. Complete the square to see its smallest value.

steps.title: Say why it is positive
steps.say: A square is never negative, so $3(x + 1)^2 \ge 0$ for every $x$. Adding $2$ makes the whole thing at least $2$.

lines.text: So $f'(x) > 0$ for all $x$, and $f$ is increasing for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

higher.tip: The answer must come from differentiating. Without $f'(x)$ you get no credit.

sources.quote: solution must be based on differentiation in order for any credit
